scenes.heading: What pH measures
scenes.narration: Every water based solution contains hydrogen ions, and pH is simply the number we use to record how crowded with those hydrogen ions a particular solution really is.

scenes.heading: The zero to fourteen scale
scenes.narration: The familiar scale runs from 0 up to 14. Pure water sits exactly at 7, and chemists call that midpoint neutral because acid and base effects balance each other perfectly.

scenes.heading: Acidic and basic sides
scenes.narration: Readings below 7 mean the solution is acidic, with lemon juice near 2. Readings above 7 mean it is basic, also called alkaline, with household bleach sitting close to 13.

scenes.heading: Each step multiplies tenfold
scenes.narration: Here is the part that matters most. The scale is logarithmic, so every single step changes the hydrogen ion concentration by 10 times. Moving from 5 to 3 means a hundredfold jump.

scenes.heading: Putting it together
scenes.narration: So pH counts hydrogen ions on a 0 to 14 logarithmic scale, 7 is neutral, lower is acidic, higher is basic, and each step is a full 10 times change.
